[Serious] What is the appeal of DOTA & DOTA2?

MOBAs in general are pretty popular, particularly with people who are into professional-level competition (whether that's actually competing at that level or just spectating competitions at that level). It's kinda popular for the same reason that CS:S was popular back in the day. Something about the multiplayer just makes you want to keep playing it. And of course ranked games allow you to actually have some metric to compare yourself to other players, so there's the desire to improve so you can go "haha, I'm better than you".

I can't speak for everyone who enjoys Dota 2, I can only give you reasons why I love it. My reasons may differ from others, but here's why Dota 2 is my addiction.

1) Complexity

Dota 2, like most other MOBA's, are some of the most complex games you can play. To be the best, you really need to know the heroes, their strengths, their weaknesses, you need to know the map inside and out, you need to know the items, what heroes work well with others, which counters the enemies heroes, etc. Dota 2 really is a game about skill. That complexity is what draws me to it. And this complexity is why no two games are the same even though it's always on the same map. It's like chess: Learn how to play in 5 minutes, takes a life time to master it.

2) Community

Yes, people will trash talk. People will yell 'GG' all because you got one last hit as a support in the laning phase. People will curse you because they died. People are assholes. That's not the community I'm talking about. When I say community, I mean those who create content and have created hubs and fan bases. Places like Dota Cinema and people like JimBen really make me love the game. The videos that they create are of great quality not just visually, but entertainment-wise, as well. So, when I say "community" I mean those who have created communities around Dota 2.

3) The free loot

The fact that you can get random item and set drops just for playing is great. Just buy playing you can get enough random item drops that if you were to sell them all, you could turn around and buy some other game on Steam. While most drops only go for a few cents, sometimes you might get a set that's worth 30 dollars on the market (A friend one time got a Lina set that was worth 32 dollars. One time I got a Spirit Breaker set worth 11 dollars).

4) Reborn

The new Reborn client is amazing, even though it's not even close to being done. The biggest thing is the Custom Games. The thing that made Warcraft 3's life last longer than it should have was the modding community. They created so many custom game mods for W3 that it never got board. Valve introduced the same thing to Dota 2. With Custom Games you can play games that are not Dota 2 but done with Dota 2 assets.

5) Linux support

For me, this is huge. I'm a Linux gamer and so for me, there aren't many MOBA's on Linux. HoN, Strife, Awesomenauts, and TOME are just about it. It just makes it even better that Dota 2 is the second largest MOBA out there AND runs natively on Linux.

6) The competitive scene

The first time I saw The International it felt like the Superbowl but for gamers. It was amazing watching it for the first time. It felt like watching any other team sports on TV. Furthermore, to see that Dota 2 has the largest prize pool of any competitive video game tournament is just insane. Just recently they reach 15 million dollars prize pool for this years TI5 and it's still going up.

Those are my reasons for loving Dota 2. There are some other things like team work, regular patches, and what not. But for me, those 6 reasons are the main reasons why Dota 2 is my addiction.

I worked on a first response ambulance from ages 13-17. AMAA

How did you manage to get that job?

Also, craziest thing you've seen working?

It was a volunteer program in our town where all three first response ambulances were run by high school students. We covered a town of about 20,000 people and seven miles of state highway.

There were a few crazy things. We saw a lot of car accidents since the highway portion we covered was windy and was prone to black ice during the winter. But one of the calls that stuck with me the most was when we were dispatched for a guy who fell off the treadmill. The gym was less than a quarter mile from our hq, so we got over there pretty quickly. We still managed to get there after the cops though since they had been in the parking lot for the gym trying to catch people speeding. We grab our basic gear (jump kit, o2 bag, and the backboard since he fell), and start heading in.

As I'm about to close the ambulance door, I hear something over the police radio inside the bus that sounded like "no pulse". So we grab the defib and run in. We get directed up the main stairs, and come upon two cops doing CPR on an older man whose face is barely recognizable. Turns out it wasn't just a fall; the guy had gone in to cardiac arrest while jogging and smashed his face on the treadmill on his way down. We were able to shock him back into sinus rhythm, and we did our best to get an airway through the broken nose and spewing blood.

We're able to get him on the backboard easy enough, but since the elevator wasn't large enough (it was big enough to fit a stretcher, but only when it was in the seated position), we had to carry him down the main flight of stairs. I still can't imagine what people were thinking when they saw three teenage girls, a teenage boy, and two cops trying to carry a 200 pound man down a spiral staircase.

We managed to get him into the bus pretty quickly, and as we were packing up to go and scheduling a medic intercept, we started to hear shouting outside of the ambulance. Turns out his wife and daughter were at the grocery store next door picking up a birthday cake for the daughter... whose birthday was that day. The wife told us that her husband had just been given a clean bill of health from his cardiologist the week before. The cops went outside the ambulance to try to calm her down, but when they opened the back doors and she saw that teenagers were the ones that were working on her husband, she went wild. She kept yelling "I don't want you fucking kids touching my husband! I want adults!". I'll never forget the confident, stern look on the cops face when he pulled her away and said "Ma'am, these kids just saved your husbands life."

Within ten minutes he was at the local hospital, and swept away to the cardiac lab for tests.

Now usually, we would drop off the patients, write a run report, and that would be the last we hear of them. But just a few months later me and my crew were brought back to the local hospital for recognition of "Call of the Year". We were among three other local ambulance crews, all of whom were well over twice our age. It was incredible to be given that kind of respect and recognition at such a young age.

A few months after that, it was time for our senior graduation ceremony. We were told we were going to have a special guest at the banquet, but I never even expected to see the same man who I had seen pulseless on the floor of a gym just months before. I can't even begin to describe the feeling of hugging someone, and feeling their heart beating, when the last time you saw them they were barely clinging on to life.

I also have some gruesome and actually insane people stories I can share, but that to me is the craziest call.

I have lots of respect for all in your line of work, sacrificing your time and mental sanity, giving all of your best so that others may live! Mad props to the cop too for recognizing that you guys knew what you were doing.
sorry, just to get that straight, you where 13 years old when you started to work for an ambulance? but you did had a medical education or what was your function? so many questions right now :)

Yeah, I know, it sounds crazy! I started out with first aid training, and just rode along on the ambulance getting equipment for the EMTs. Part of my job was also to man the town radio and listen into the police/fire stations for possible medical calls. When I was 15 I took the EMT course and was officially certified on my 16th birthday (I had finished the course a few months before hand, but had to wait until I was 16 since that's the minimum age for an EMT in my state). When I was 17 I became the driver. Our function was to cover the three first response ambulances in our town. The entire program was staffed by high schoolers.

this is amazing, when i was 13 i felt like a badass when i beat the endboss of super metroid on SNES... while you where driving around, saving peoples life...wow. where are you from? does that programm still exists?

We used to play guitar hero between calls, and sometimes I got more satisfaction out of getting a perfect score on a song than a call I was just on :). I grew up in Connecticut and yep, it's still around! It's been around since 1970. We've had a few other towns come by our hq to see how it works in order to start one of their own, but none have succeeded. Their lack of success is because they didn't give full responsibility to the kids. Sure, we had adults supervising, but we would do all the work. We'd organize our own shifts, keep the kitchens and supply rooms stocked, write our own reports, build our own databases, and dole out our own punishments for doing something wrong (missing a meeting, being late for a shift, etc).
Having that experience as such a young child sounds amazing. How has it impacted your outlook as an adult?

Having such a huge responsibility at such a young age help give me confidence in what I do, even if I'm the youngest one in the room. It taught me that your age doesn't have to relate to knowledge or experience. I've always loved the quote "It's not the years in your life that count. It's the life in your years".

Initially, simply because I went to college. But the reason I didn't go back is that I wanted to branch out and explore more fields. I always get an itch to go back and work on an ambulance again though.
Very impressive. Did anyone ever look down on you for being so young?

Most of the people in the town I served knew of the program, and weren't caught off guard when we showed up. The only person I've experienced in the town that looked down on us initially was the woman I mentioned in the story I told here.

But we also covered seven miles of a major interstate, where no one would ever expect to call 911 and have high schoolers show up. We would get some backlash there, but most of the time people were so injured that I don't think they even registered that we were so young.
